title: Assignments
text:
The main idea is the lack of attention that statistical textbooks and software pay to graphics.
Three red flags:

It is wrong to assume that numeric calculations are correct and graphs are the “weird” part.
There is not one single way to analyze the data.
There is no virtue in just taking into account the calculus.

Given that:

Before every calculation, provide the scatterplot.
Plot the residuals against the adjusted (fitted) values after the regression.
Outlier — always investigate. Is it an error? Report it.
If the curves suggest non-linearity, consider transformations.




The default color was replaced with a custom sky-blue tone (skyblue).




In April 2014, Reuters published a graphic on the number of gun deaths in Florida, with the “Stand Your Ground” law (2005) as the turning point. However, the Y-axis was inverted, which conveyed a decrease in the numbers when the opposite was true. The numbers were not wrong — the form was. The solution is simple: keep the Y-axis in its conventional position.
Source: “How to Mislead With Charts” — Pacific Standard




Base R Graphics: Murrell chapter 1 and the Happy Planet Index



Assignment 3: Anatomy of a Chart



The Limits of Big Data and the Grammar of Graphics

title: Assignment 2: Base R Graphics
text:
I ran the author’s code for Figures 1.1 and 1.2 (https://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/~paul/RG3e/chapter1.html) line by line. The DEVICE: comments note what changed on the device after each call. The code’s comments pose no questions.


Code
set.seed(1)
## Murrell, R Graphics (3rd ed.), chapter 1 - Figures 1.1 and 1.2
## Annotated walk-through: run ONE line at a time (Ctrl+Enter) and watch the
## Plots pane. "DEVICE:" notes say what changes after each call.

## ---- Figure 1.1: a simple scatterplot --------------------------------------
plot(pressure)
# DEVICE: new page; axes, box, labels and 19 points (temperature vs pressure).
text(150, 600, "Pressure (mm Hg)\nversus\nTemperature (Celsius)")
# DEVICE: nothing is erased; the text is added at DATA coordinates (x=150, y=600).
# "\n" breaks the label into three lines.

## ---- Figure 1.2: six standard plots on one page ---------------------------
par(mfrow = c(3, 2))
# DEVICE: nothing visible yet - the page is now split into a 3 x 2 grid,
# and each new high-level plot fills the next cell (row by row).

## (1) Scatterplot built piece by piece ------------------------------------
x  <- c(0.5, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16)
y1 <- c(1, 1.3, 1.9, 3.4, 3.9, 4.8)
y2 <- c(4, .8, .5, .45, .4, .3)
par(las = 1, mar = c(4, 4, 2, 4), cex = .7)
# DEVICE: nothing drawn; horizontal tick labels, wider right margin (for axis 4),
# smaller text.
plot.new()
# DEVICE: moves to cell 1 - an EMPTY plot region (no axes, no box).
plot.window(range(x), c(0, 6))
# DEVICE: still blank; only sets the coordinate system (x range, y 0-6).
lines(x, y1)
lines(x, y2)
# DEVICE: two lines appear, no axes yet.
points(x, y1, pch = 16, cex = 2)
# DEVICE: large filled circles on line 1.
points(x, y2, pch = 21, bg = "white", cex = 2)
# DEVICE: large open circles (white fill hides the line under them) on line 2.
par(col = "gray50", fg = "gray50", col.axis = "gray50")
# DEVICE: nothing yet; what is drawn next will be grey.
axis(1, at = seq(0, 16, 4))
axis(2, at = seq(0, 6, 2))
axis(4, at = seq(0, 6, 2))
# DEVICE: grey axes on bottom (1), left (2) and right (4) sides.
box(bty = "u")
# DEVICE: a U-shaped frame (left, bottom, right - no top line).
mtext("Travel Time (s)", side = 1, line = 2, cex = 0.8)
mtext("Responses per Travel", side = 2, line = 2, las = 0, cex = 0.8)
mtext("Responses per Second", side = 4, line = 2, las = 0, cex = 0.8)
# DEVICE: axis titles written in the MARGINS (line = distance from the plot).
text(4, 5, "Bird 131")
# DEVICE: label inside the plot, at data coordinates (4, 5).
par(mar = c(5.1, 4.1, 4.1, 2.1), col = "black", fg = "black", col.axis = "black")
# DEVICE: nothing; restores default margins and colours.

## (2) Histogram with density curve --------------------------------------
Y <- rnorm(50)
Y[Y < -3.5 | Y > 3.5] <- NA
x  <- seq(-3.5, 3.5, .1)
dn <- dnorm(x)
par(mar = c(4.5, 4.1, 3.1, 0))
hist(Y, breaks = seq(-3.5, 3.5), ylim = c(0, 0.5), col = "gray80", freq = FALSE)
# DEVICE: cell 2 - histogram of 50 random normals; freq = FALSE puts DENSITY on y.
lines(x, dnorm(x), lwd = 2)
# DEVICE: the theoretical normal curve is laid over the bars.
# (Run it again: the bars change, because rnorm() draws new random numbers.)
par(mar = c(5.1, 4.1, 4.1, 2.1))

## (3) Stacked barplot ---------------------------------------------------
par(mar = c(2, 3.1, 2, 2.1))
midpts <- barplot(VADeaths, col = gray(0.1 + seq(1, 9, 2)/11),
                  names = rep("", 4))
# DEVICE: cell 3 - four stacked bars, five grey shades, no group labels.
# barplot() also RETURNS the x-position of each bar's centre (midpts).
mtext(sub(" ", "\n", colnames(VADeaths)),
      at = midpts, side = 1, line = 0.5, cex = 0.5)
# DEVICE: group names written under each bar on two lines ("Rural\nMale").
text(rep(midpts, each = 5), apply(VADeaths, 2, cumsum) - VADeaths/2,
     VADeaths, col = rep(c("white", "black"), times = 3:2), cex = 0.8)
# DEVICE: each segment's value written in its middle; white text on the
# three dark segments, black on the two light ones.
par(mar = c(5.1, 4.1, 4.1, 2.1))

## (4) Side-by-side boxplots ---------------------------------------------
par(mar = c(3, 4.1, 2, 0))
boxplot(len ~ dose, data = ToothGrowth,
        boxwex = 0.25, at = 1:3 - 0.2,
        subset = supp == "VC", col = "white",
        xlab = "", ylab = "tooth length", ylim = c(0, 35))
# DEVICE: cell 4 - three narrow white boxes (Vitamin C), shifted LEFT by 0.2.
mtext("Vitamin C dose (mg)", side = 1, line = 2.5, cex = 0.8)
boxplot(len ~ dose, data = ToothGrowth, add = TRUE,
        boxwex = 0.25, at = 1:3 + 0.2,
        subset = supp == "OJ")
# DEVICE: add = TRUE draws on the SAME plot: grey boxes (orange juice)
# shifted RIGHT by 0.2, so each dose shows a pair.
legend(1.5, 9, c("Ascorbic acid", "Orange juice"),
       fill = c("white", "gray"), bty = "n")
# DEVICE: key at (1.5, 9), no border around it (bty = "n").
par(mar = c(5.1, 4.1, 4.1, 2.1))

## (5) Perspective (3-D) plot ------------------------------------------
x <- seq(-10, 10, length = 30)
y <- x
f <- function(x, y) { r <- sqrt(x^2 + y^2); 10 * sin(r)/r }
z <- outer(x, y, f)
z[is.na(z)] <- 1
# (sin(0)/0 is NaN at the centre; it is replaced by the limit value.)
par(mar = c(0, 0.5, 0, 0), lwd = 0.5)
persp(x, y, z, theta = 30, phi = 30, expand = 0.5)
# DEVICE: cell 5 - the "sombrero" surface; theta turns it left/right,
# phi tilts it up/down, expand squashes the height.
par(mar = c(5.1, 4.1, 4.1, 2.1), lwd = 1)

## (6) Pie chart ---------------------------------------------------------
par(mar = c(0, 2, 1, 2), xpd = FALSE, cex = 0.5)
pie.sales <- c(0.12, 0.3, 0.26, 0.16, 0.04, 0.12)
names(pie.sales) <- c("Blueberry", "Cherry", "Apple",
                      "Boston Cream", "Other", "Vanilla")
# names() draws nothing: it only attaches labels to the vector,
# and pie() then uses those names as slice labels.
pie(pie.sales, col = gray(seq(0.3, 1.0, length = 6)))
# DEVICE: cell 6 - six grey slices, labelled from names(pie.sales).
par(mar = c(5.1, 4.1, 4.1, 2.1), xpd = FALSE, cex = 1, mfrow = c(1, 1))
# DEVICE: back to one plot per page for what follows.








Figure 1











Figure 2

title: Assignment 2: Base R Graphics
text:
2. Data: the Happy Planet Index
Source: Abdallah, S. & Barberà Mas, E. (2026). The Happy Planet Index 2026 Data File. Hot or Cool Institute. https://happyplanetindex.org.
Year: 2025. I chose 2025 because it is the most recent year in the release. It covers 134 countries.
names() is used only to give the columns short names; it is not a graphics function.


Code
library(readxl)
## Data: HPI 2026 data file, sheet "1. All countries" (year selected: 2025).
## The first 8 rows are titles; the column names are in row 9.
hpi <- read_excel("Data/HPI_public_dataset.xlsx",
                  sheet = "1. All countries", skip = 8)
hpi <- hpi[, 1:12]
names(hpi) <- c("rank", "country", "iso", "blank", "continent", "pop",
                "lifeexp", "satisf", "footprint", "hpi", "threshold", "gdp")
hpi <- hpi[!is.na(hpi$country) & !is.na(hpi$hpi), ]
hpi$continent <- factor(hpi$continent, levels = 1:8,
                        labels = c("Latin America", "N. America & Oceania",
                                   "Western Europe", "Middle East & N. Africa",
                                   "Sub-Saharan Africa", "South Asia",
                                   "E. Europe & Central Asia", "East Asia"))
nrow(hpi)


[1] 134

title: Assignment 2: Base R Graphics
text:
3. The plotting functions

a. Set up the canvas

par()
par() sets graphical parameters for the plots that follow; here mfrow = c(1, 2) puts two plots side by side.


Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(hpi$satisf, hpi$hpi, xlab = "Life satisfaction", ylab = "HPI")
plot(hpi$footprint, hpi$hpi, xlab = "Ecological footprint", ylab = "HPI")









Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))




box()
box() draws the frame around the plot region; bty = "l" keeps only the left and bottom sides.


Code
plot(hpi$lifeexp, hpi$hpi, axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "Life expectancy", ylab = "HPI")
axis(1)
axis(2)
box(bty = "l")











axis()
axis() draws one axis and controls where its tick marks go and how they are labelled.


Code
plot(hpi$gdp, hpi$hpi, log = "x", axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "GDP per capita (log scale)", ylab = "HPI")
axis(1, at = c(1000, 10000, 100000), labels = c("$1k", "$10k", "$100k"))
axis(2)
box()












b. Draw whole plots

hist()
hist() divides a numeric variable into bins and draws how many observations fall in each.


Code
hist(hpi$hpi, col = "gray80", xlab = "HPI", main = "HPI scores, 2025")











boxplot()
boxplot() shows the median, quartiles and outliers of a variable for each group.


Code
par(mar = c(4, 11, 2, 1))
boxplot(hpi ~ continent, data = hpi, horizontal = TRUE, las = 1,
        xlab = "HPI", ylab = "")









Code
par(mar = c(5.1, 4.1, 4.1, 2.1))




pie()
pie() divides a circle into slices proportional to a set of values.


Code
pie(table(hpi$continent), main = "Countries by continent")











persp()
persp() draws a 3-D surface seen from an angle set by theta and phi; here the density of countries by life expectancy and footprint.


Code
dens <- MASS::kde2d(hpi$lifeexp, hpi$footprint)
persp(dens$x, dens$y, dens$z, theta = -30, phi = 30,
      xlab = "Life expectancy", ylab = "Footprint", zlab = "Density")












c. Add to an existing plot

points()
points() adds points to an existing plot; here Brazil in red.


Code
plot(hpi$footprint, hpi$hpi, col = "gray",
     xlab = "Ecological footprint", ylab = "HPI")
br <- hpi$country == "Brazil"
points(hpi$footprint[br], hpi$hpi[br], pch = 16, col = "red", cex = 2)











lines()
lines() adds connected lines to an existing plot; here a lowess trend.


Code
plot(hpi$footprint, hpi$hpi, xlab = "Ecological footprint", ylab = "HPI")
lines(lowess(hpi$footprint, hpi$hpi), lwd = 2)












d. Annotate

text()
text() writes text inside the plot at given coordinates; here two country names.


Code
plot(hpi$satisf, hpi$lifeexp, xlab = "Life satisfaction",
     ylab = "Life expectancy")
sel <- hpi$country %in% c("Brazil", "Costa Rica")
text(hpi$satisf[sel], hpi$lifeexp[sel], hpi$country[sel], pos = 2)











mtext()
mtext() writes text in the margins of the plot; here the data source.


Code
plot(hpi$satisf, hpi$hpi, xlab = "Life satisfaction", ylab = "HPI")
mtext("Source: Happy Planet Index 2026", side = 1, line = 4, adj = 0)











legend()
legend() adds a key that explains colours or symbols; here the continents.


Code
plot(hpi$footprint, hpi$hpi, col = hpi$continent, pch = 16,
     xlab = "Ecological footprint", ylab = "HPI")
legend("topright", legend = levels(hpi$continent), col = 1:8, pch = 16,
       cex = 0.7)

title: Assignment 3 - EPPS 6356
text:
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)

# Daily COVID counts, Our World in Data.
url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/owid/covid-19-data/",
              "master/public/data/owid-covid-data.csv")
download.file(url, "owid-covid-data.csv")
owidall <- read.csv("owid-covid-data.csv")

# Drop OWID aggregate rows (continents, income groups, World)
owidall <- owidall[!grepl("^OWID", owidall$iso_code), ]

# Subset by continent
owideu <- subset(owidall, continent == "Europe")
owideu$date <- as.Date(owideu$date)

# Removing Russia since it seems to be absent in the graph template
df <- dplyr::filter(owideu,
                    !is.na(new_deaths),
                    location != "Russia")





q3 <- quantile(df$new_deaths, 0.75, na.rm=T)
iqr <- IQR(df$new_deaths)
sup <- q3 + 1.5*iqr
df$outliers <- ifelse(df$new_deaths > sup, df$location, NA)





ggplot(df)+
  aes(x=date, y=new_deaths)+
  geom_point(col='#E7298A')+
  #geom_text(aes(label=outliers), na.rm=T)+
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "2 months",
    date_labels = "%Y-%m"
    )+
  labs(title = "Daily COVID deaths in Europe",
       y = "COVID Deaths in Europe (Daily)",
       x = "Date")+
  #scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,6600))+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle=90, vjust=0.5, hjust=1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

text:
I reran murrell01.R in full. Then I chose the “Bird 131” scatterplot.


Code
# Data: travel time (x) and two response measures (y1, y2).
x  <- c(0.5, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16)
y1 <- c(1, 1.3, 1.9, 3.4, 3.9, 4.8)
y2 <- c(4, .8, .5, .45, .4, .3)

# Horizontal axis labels, margins (bottom, left, top, right) and smaller text.
# The right margin is bigger to fit a second y axis.
par(las = 1, mar = c(4, 4, 2, 4), cex = .7)

# Opens an empty plot. Nothing is drawn yet.
plot.new()

# Sets the x and y ranges. Nothing is drawn yet.
plot.window(range(x), c(0, 6))

# Draws the line for y1.
lines(x, y1)

# Draws the line for y2.
lines(x, y2)

# Adds black filled points to y1 (pch = 16), twice the size (cex = 2).
points(x, y1, pch = 16, cex = 2)

# Adds open points to y2 (pch = 21) with a white inside (bg).
# Filled and open points show the two series without a legend.
points(x, y2, pch = 21, bg = "white", cex = 2)

# From here on, axes and labels are gray, so the data stands out.
par(col = "gray50", fg = "gray50", col.axis = "gray50")

# x axis at the bottom (side 1).
axis(1, at = seq(0, 16, 4))

# y axis on the left (side 2).
axis(2, at = seq(0, 6, 2))

# y axis on the right (side 4).
axis(4, at = seq(0, 6, 2))

# Frame around the plot, open at the top ("u" shape).
box(bty = "u")

# x axis title, in the bottom margin.
mtext("Travel Time (s)", side = 1, line = 2, cex = 0.8)

# Left y axis title; las = 0 makes it vertical.
mtext("Responses per Travel", side = 2, line = 2, las = 0, cex = 0.8)

# Right y axis title, also vertical.
mtext("Responses per Second", side = 4, line = 2, las = 0, cex = 0.8)

# Label inside the plot, at x = 4 and y = 5.
text(4, 5, "Bird 131")

# Resets margins and colors to the default.
par(mar = c(5.1, 4.1, 4.1, 2.1), col = "black", fg = "black",
    col.axis = "black")

2. Anscombe’s quartet
I reran anscombe01.R in full.

Regression models


Code
# Fit one linear regression for each of the four sets.
lm1 <- lm(y1 ~ x1, data = anscombe)
lm2 <- lm(y2 ~ x2, data = anscombe)
lm3 <- lm(y3 ~ x3, data = anscombe)
lm4 <- lm(y4 ~ x4, data = anscombe)


The numbers below come from summary(lm1) to summary(lm4).




Set 1
Set 2
Set 3
Set 4




Intercept
3.0001

Slope
0.5001
0.500

R²
0.6665

0.6667


Residual standard error
1.237
1.237

The four models are almost identical: y ≈ 3 + 0.5x, with the same R² and the same error.


Four ways to draw them


Code
# Four plots on one page: 2 rows, 2 columns.
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

# Set 1: blue circles, solid line.
plot(anscombe$x1, anscombe$y1, col = "blue", pch = 16,
     xlim = c(3, 19), ylim = c(3, 13), xlab = "x1", ylab = "y1")
abline(lm1, col = "gray40", lty = 1, lwd = 2)

# Set 2: green triangles, dashed line.
plot(anscombe$x2, anscombe$y2, col = "forestgreen", pch = 17,
     xlim = c(3, 19), ylim = c(3, 13), xlab = "x2", ylab = "y2")
abline(lm2, col = "gray40", lty = 2, lwd = 2)

# Set 3: yellow squares, dotted line.
plot(anscombe$x3, anscombe$y3, col = "gold", pch = 15,
     xlim = c(3, 19), ylim = c(3, 13), xlab = "x3", ylab = "y3")
abline(lm3, col = "gray40", lty = 3, lwd = 2)

# Set 4: red diamonds, dot-dash line.
plot(anscombe$x4, anscombe$y4, col = "red", pch = 18,
     xlim = c(3, 19), ylim = c(3, 13), xlab = "x4", ylab = "y4")
abline(lm4, col = "gray40", lty = 4, lwd = 2)

# Back to one plot per page.
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))








Figure 2: Anscombe’s quartet: same regression line, four different patterns.





Comparing the drawings.
Professor’s version: - same style in all four plots: orange points and a blue line.
My version: - each set has its own color, its own symbol, and its own line type.
What the summary statistics hide. The four regressions have the same intercept (3), slope (0.5), R² (0.67) and residual standard error (1.24). The plots show:

Set 1: a normal linear relationship, with points around the line.
Set 2: a curve. A straight line is the wrong model.
Set 3: an almost perfect line, but one outlier pulls the regression line up.
Set 4: almost all points have x = 8. One single point at x = 19 creates the whole line.

Same numbers, four stories. Always plot the data before trusting the statistics.

title: Assignment 3: Anatomy of a Chart
text:
4. Now do it in ggplot2
I reproduced the tuned chart from Part 3 with ggplot2.


Code
library(tidyverse)
windowsFonts(Garamond = windowsFont("Garamond"))
lm1 <- lm(y1 ~ x1, data = anscombe)

ggplot(anscombe, aes(x = x1, y = y1)) +
  geom_text(label = "E", family = "Garamond", colour = "darkblue", size = 6) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(lm1)[1], slope = coef(lm1)[2],
              colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(4, 14, 2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 4:11) +
  labs(title = "Anscombe's Set 1", x = "x1", y = "y1") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(text = element_text(family = "Garamond"),
        plot.title = element_text(colour = "darkblue", face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
        axis.title = element_text(colour = "gray30"),
        axis.text = element_text(colour = "gray30"),
        panel.grid = element_blank())








Figure 4





Became theme() arguments: the font (family in par() became text = element_text(family = ...)), the title color (col.main became plot.title), the axis label color (col.lab became axis.title) and the axis number color (col.axis became axis.text).
Became scale_*(): the tick marks on the axes, which base R chose by itself, became scale_x_continuous(breaks = ...) and scale_y_continuous(breaks = ...).
No equivalent: windowsFonts() and par() have no ggplot2 version. Also, pch = "E" had no direct match: geom_point(shape = "E") ignores the theme font, so I used geom_text().

title: Research
text:
Beyond the Bars: A Study of Recidivism Among Texas Inmates and the Influence of Sentence Length Master’s Thesis in Criminology, The University of Texas at Dallas, 2025 — Supervising Professor: Tony Love, PhD

This thesis examines the relationship between prison sentence length and the likelihood of rearrest or reincarceration among first-time inmates released from Texas state prisons. Using logistic regression, it finds that moderately long sentences (2–10 years) significantly increase recidivism, while very long sentences (25+ years) show no significant effect relative to shorter sentences — challenging deterrence theory and the presumed benefits of incapacitation.

Data-generating process. The data come from the Windham School District Biennial Evaluation project, an administrative dataset tracking first-time inmates released from Texas state prisons between September 2017 and May 2019 (N = 45,744). Records were compiled to evaluate the relationship between sentence length and reincarceration, with sentence length grouped into four bands and recidivism defined as rearrest or reincarceration within a set follow-up window.

title: Class 5 Note: The Limits of Big Data and the Grammar of Graphics
text:
Google Flu Trends (GFT), launched in 2008, estimated flu activity in the United States from the volume of Google searches, one to two weeks ahead of the CDC reports (Ginsberg et al., 2009). It then missed the 2009 H1N1 pandemic and, in 2012–13, predicted more than double the doctor visits the CDC recorded; from August 2011 it overestimated flu in 100 of 108 weeks (Lazer et al., 2014).
What strikes me most is the arrogance of the claim. Lazer et al. call it “big data hubris”: the assumption that big data can replace, rather than supplement, traditional data collection and analysis. Google assumed its data were better than the existing model without explaining how or why. That is an argument from authority, and it does not belong in science. In fact, a simple model using lagged CDC data predicted better than GFT.
Two other problems follow. The first is algorithm dynamics: Google kept changing its own search engine, for example by suggesting related searches, and users changed their behaviour, so the process generating the data changed under the model. The second is transparency and replicability: Google never disclosed the search terms or the full method, so nobody outside the company could reproduce or correct the results.

title: Class 5 Note: The Limits of Big Data and the Grammar of Graphics
text:
b. Overfitting and overparameterization
Overfitting happens when a model fits the noise of the data it was trained on: it performs very well on the data it has seen and badly on new data. Overparameterization is the condition that invites it: more parameters, or more candidate predictors, than the data can support. GFT had both. Its engineers screened about 50 million search terms against only 1,152 CDC data points, so some terms matched the flu curve by pure chance, such as searches about high school basketball, which simply shares the winter season with flu (Lazer et al., 2014).
My own field offers a parallel. Research on social disorganization explains crime partly by residential turnover and by the presence of many cultures in one neighbourhood. These studies usually put all Latino immigrants in one box. But Latino is much more than Mexico: Brazil, Costa Rica and Argentina are very different cultures, and what holds for one group does not necessarily hold for another. This is not overfitting in the strict statistical sense, but the failure is the same: a pattern learned from one sample is assumed to hold for people the model has never seen.
The chart below shows overfitting with simulated data. As the polynomial degree increases, the training error keeps falling, while the error on new data falls up to degree 4 and then rises.


Code
## Overfitting: training vs. test error as polynomial degree increases
set.seed(2)
x <- runif(20, 0, 10)                        # 20 training points
y <- sin(x) + rnorm(20, sd = 0.4)
x_new <- runif(100, 0, 10)                   # 100 new points, same process
y_new <- sin(x_new) + rnorm(100, sd = 0.4)

degree <- 1:10
train_err <- test_err <- numeric(10)
for (d in degree) {
  fit <- lm(y ~ poly(x, d))
  train_err[d] <- mean((y - predict(fit))^2)
  test_err[d]  <- mean((y_new - predict(fit, data.frame(x = x_new)))^2)
}

plot(degree, train_err, type = "b", pch = 16, log = "y",
     ylim = range(train_err, test_err),
     xlab = "Polynomial degree", ylab = "Mean squared error (log scale)",
     main = "Overfitting: training vs. test error")
lines(degree, test_err, type = "b", pch = 1, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Training error", "Test error"),
       pch = c(16, 1), lty = c(1, 2))








Figure 1: Training error always falls with model complexity; test error does not.

title: Class 5 Note: The Limits of Big Data and the Grammar of Graphics
text:
c. Wickham talk summary
In his EMBL keynote, Hadley Wickham presents R and the tidyverse: tidy data (tidyr), data transformation with dplyr and the pipe, ggplot2 and its grammar of graphics, and extensions such as gganimate and ggseg. He rebuilds the Gapminder bubble chart step by step and makes four main points. First, data must be tidy, with one variable per column, before any chart is possible. Second, a plot is made of independent (“orthogonal”) components (data, aesthetic mappings, geoms, scales) that can be changed one at a time and combined across packages written by different people. Third, visualization is iterative: he compares his first draft with the original and asks “what’s missing?”. Fourth, code is the right medium because it is text, readable and reproducible, which is exactly what Google Flu Trends was not.
I would qualify three points. “Code is readable” holds for those who already program; coming from the humanities and social sciences, I found the entry barrier real. I also doubt that one must make something bad in order to make something good: a first version can be good and the next ones better. Finally, the animation is impressive, but it makes precise comparison between years difficult.
